title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks, and Runbooks
author: Ava Morgan
body:
Overview:

This document consolidates the serving runtime reference for Redwood Inference: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling and performance playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and team ownership. It is intended for engineers who operate or extend the serving runtime, SREs responsible for production SLOs, and performance/benchmarking engineers onboarding new models or hardware.

1) High-level runtime architecture

Summary:
- The serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine responsible for executing model inference with low latency and high throughput across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Key responsibilities: request routing, batching, kernel selection, KV cache management, quantization-aware execution, telemetry, and graceful fallback.

Components (logical):
- Frontend API Layer: REST/gRPC entry points, authentication, rate limiting, request validation.
- Router & Policy Engine: routes requests to pools based on latency/cost/tier/region policies.
- Scheduler & Batcher: continuous batching service that creates microbatches respecting latency SLOs and priority.
- Execution Engine: per-GPU process that loads model artifacts, manages KV cache, selects kernels and CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN/cuFFT kernels or Triton-backed paths.
- Telemetry & Tracing: token-level latency, memory usage, kernel timings, and tail-latency histograms.
- Persistence & Metadata: model catalog metadata, quantization profile store, and rollout/version config.

Sequence flow (high-level):
1. Request received at Frontend; metadata annotated (model, prompt length, customer tier).
2. Router evaluates policy and forwards to a candidate pool.
3. Scheduler groups requests into a microbatch; batching policy ensures SLOs.
4. Execution Engine selects optimized kernel path and executes.
5. KV cache consulted and updated as needed; streaming tokens returned to caller.
6. Telemetry emitted and aggregated into per-route dashboards.

2) Kernel scheduling design

Goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization while meeting per-request latency SLOs (P95/P99 targets).
- Prefer lower-cost kernels for short sequences; switch to high-throughput kernels for long sequences or large batches.

Scheduling primitives:
- Microbatch windows: configurable (default 3ms) that allow short coalescing without increasing tail latency.
- Priority queues: low/normal/high request priorities; high priority bypasses batching where defined.
- Kernel selector: rules + cost model to choose between execution paths (float16 fp16 kernel, int8 quantized kernel, fused attention kernels, Triton fused kernels).
- Preemption: long-running kernels can be preempted if a higher-priority request arrives and preemption budget allows.

Practical rules and thresholds (examples):
- If median sequence length < 32 tokens and predicted latency budget < 30ms, prefer fp16 single-stream kernels.
- If batch_size >= 8 and average sequence_length >= 128, prefer fused attention kernels or Triton multi-stream kernels.
- For quantized models (int8), only select int8 path when model profile has accuracy delta <= 0.5% measured on canonical eval set.

Operational knobs:
- microbatch_window_ms (default 3)
- max_microbatch_size (default 32)
- priority_bypass_threshold_ms (default 10)
- kernel_selector_model (cost model name)

3) Profiling playbook (how-to measure and triage)

Purpose: provide a repeatable process to identify latency regressions, kernel hotspots, and memory issues.

Prerequisites:
- Access to profiling cluster or dedicated GPU instance (n1-standard equivalent or private lab GPU).
- Profiling tools: perf, nvprof/nvtx (or Nsight Systems), PyTorch/TensorRT profiling hooks, and our internal kernel-timing exporter.

Steps:
1. Reproduce baseline: run the same request set locally (canonical prompt-set) and capture baseline metrics (P50/P95/P99 latencies, GPU % utilization, memory footprint).
2. Attach tracing: enable NVTX/Nsight markers around batching and kernel execution.
3. Collect kernel timelines: record kernel durations, memory copies, and synchronization points.
4. Compare to baseline: identify new or regressed kernels, increased memcpy overhead, or stall periods.
5. Hypothesize root cause: common causes are increased sequence length skew, failure to use fused kernels, KV cache thrashing, or unexpected memory growth.
6. Mitigation experiments: change microbatch_window_ms, force alternate kernel path, run with a different quantization profile, and re-profile.
7. Rollout: when mitigation verified, publish change behind feature flag and monitor for 48-72 hours.

Checklist (triage):
- Is the regression limited to a single model or global?
- Are particular GPUs/nodes exhibiting higher latencies?
- Is there an increase in memcpy or PCIe traffic?
- Any recent rollout (model change, kernel upgrade, CUDA driver update)?

4) Benchmarking suite (how and when to run)

Scope:
- Unit benchmarks: single-GPU kernel latency and memory usage for representative shapes.
- End-to-end benchmarks: simulated traffic with production routing rules measuring P50/P95/P99, throughput, and cost-per-token.
- Regression harness: nightly runs against canonical prompt sets and sample real-customer workloads.

Running benchmarks:
- Tooling: use the internal bench-runner (bench-runner CLI) with config YAMLs stored in /repo/bench/configs/. Example command:
  bench-runner run --config configs/llama-2-7b-prod.yaml --target cluster:staging --duration 30m

Benchmark outputs (collected):
- Per-kernel time series (ms)
- Batch size distribution and effective batch utilization
- Token-level cost estimate (USD/token) using current pricing model
- Memory high-water mark and fragmentation metrics

Interpreting results:
- Track delta against baseline over time. Alert on >10% P95 regression or >20% increase in cost-per-token.
- Use the benchmark outputs to update kernel_selector_model and batching heuristics.

5) Recent release notes (high level)

Release 2026-02-28 (v1.9.0 runtime):
- Improved kernel selector cost model for fused-attention kernels; P95 reduced by 12% on average for long-sequence workloads.
- Added microbatch_window_ms adaptive mode (auto-tune based on traffic patterns).
- Fixed KV cache invalidation bug that could cause memory leak during rapid model rollouts.
- New benchmark harness integration with CI to fail PRs that regress P95 > 8%.

Release 2025-12-15 (v1.8.2 runtime patch):
- Backported CUDA 12.1 driver compatibility and fixed a race in GPU memory allocator.
- Safety: flag added to prevent selecting int8 path for models without verified evals.

6) Known issues and mitigations

Issue: Sporadic P99 spikes on T4-class GPUs under mixed short/long workloads.
- Symptom: Spikes correlate with sudden long-sequence burst from a single tenant.
- Mitigation: Enable tenant-level shaping (limit long sequences per second) and enable preemption for high-priority short requests. Planned fix: kernel preemption improvements (ETA Q2 2026).

Issue: KV cache fragmentation after aggressive rollouts.
- Symptom: Memory high-water mark grows slowly after multiple model swaps.
- Mitigation: Periodic cache compaction job (cron: compaction-hourly), and ensure model teardown hooks flush caches.

Issue: Int8 path occasionally shows small quality regressions for edge prompts.
- Mitigation: Block int8 by default for customer tiers flagged as quality-sensitive; require quantization A/B for sample prompts.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

P95 latency regression (initial triage):
1. Confirm alert: check dashboards (route-level P50/P95/P99) and recent deploys.
2. Identify scope: run bench-runner against a fixed prompt-set to reproduce.
3. Collect traces: enable debug telemetry for affected route for 15 minutes (set trace-level=2).
4. If kernel hotspot: open profiling session (see Profiling playbook) and run Nsight capture.
5. If node-level: cordon node, drain workloads, and restart runtime process.
6. Rollback if deploy suspected: rollback model or runtime image and monitor for 30 minutes.

Node OOM during rollout:
1. Abort rollout and stop new rollout jobs.
2. Identify offending model(s); check memory HWM and recent artifact sizes.
3. Run cache-compaction and restart runtime on node.
4. If persistent, scale up node size or reduce max_model_replicas.

Kernel upgrade (safe rollout):
1. Validate kernels in staging with bench-runner; compare against baseline P95/P99.
2. Deploy to canary pool (5% traffic) with feature flag enabled.
3. Monitor 1h and check SLOs; if stable, increase to 25% then 100%.
4. If regression detected, revert and open a postmortem.

8) Team wiki, ownership and SLAs

Ownership:
- Runtime core: serving-runtime team (primary). Contact: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Kernel selector & profiler: perf-eng team (secondary).
- Benchmarks & CI gates: infra-perf team.

SLOs (examples):
- Route-level P95 latency: 150ms (hosted default); error budget 0.5% monthly.
- Deployment availability: 99.95% for Dedicated pools.

Knowledge base links (team wiki):
- Onboarding checklist for new runtime engineers: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-team-wiki-playbook-2026-10-10
- Bench config repo: git@repo:bench/configs

9) Appendix: example configs

Example batching config (YAML):

microbatch_window_ms: 3
max_microbatch_size: 32
priority_bypass_threshold_ms: 10
adaptive_mode: true
kernel_selector_model: "v2-cost-model"

Example bench-runner config snippet (YAML):

model: llama-2-13b-v1
traffic_profile:
  - p50: 10 rps
  - p95: 100 rps
  duration: 30m
canary_settings:
  traffic_split: [90,10]
  verify_slo: true

10) Contact and escalation

Primary oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com
Escalation path: runtime engineer -> senior runtime -> eng-sre -> CTO on-call (if >4h outage).

If you modify kernel selection heuristics or batching knobs, update this page with rationale, benchmark data, and a link to the PR that introduced the change.
